title: Commissioner Greg Sankey insists SEC breakaway threat is real as rules frustrations linger
content:
TAMPA, Fla. — SEC commissioner Greg Sankey reiterated Monday that talk of the conference breaking away is “real,” and not a leverage play.

The idea of an SEC breakaway, either to a drastic or small extent, has been simmering within the conference for a while, then broke out at SEC spring meetings in late May. Sankey did not directly address the possibility during his opening comments Monday, at the start of SEC football media days, but the first question was about how real the breakaway talk was. Notably, Sankey did not downplay it.

“They’re real,” Sankey said. “People have talked about that. They’ve opined about the frustrations that bring them to the point of saying we should look at something significantly different. I do not believe that is a leverage point. I think that’s just honest communication. … I think what’s important is those comments represent a high level of frustration in the circumstances in which we find ourselves.”

Those frustrations are largely about how national rules — tampering, the House v. NCAA settlement, eligibility — are being enforced, and whether it would be better for the SEC to adopt its own rules and potentially only play against its own schools. Sankey pointed Monday to “the frustration that exists” over different eligibility rules, and disagreements over the future format of the College Football Playoff.

But he finished his response by reiterating the preference to compete nationally, pointing to the pride he takes in the SEC’s 13 national championships in NCAA sports this past school year.

“There is meaning and value, and I do think the national expectation is that we participate in a national organization,” Sankey said. “But that national organization must function in a healthy manner. Otherwise that simmering will continue.”

Sankey also said federal legislation remains a “needed path” for college sports as a whole and that the conference is committed to getting a bill to the finish line. But he also cited “ongoing dialogue” and four broad changes the SEC is promoting to the Protect College Sports Act: legal protections, clear national standards, transparency and accountability with name, image and likeness rules and “fair and consistent standards” for conferences that also preserve institutional choice.

Sankey did not mention it directly, but one provision essentially freezes conference realignment at the Power 4 level. ESPN and Yahoo reported Monday morning that one revision under discussion would cap SEC and Big Ten membership at 19 teams. Sankey said some of the issues in the part of the bill about conference realignment and media rights are “critically important” to the SEC.

“If Congress is going to act, and again I believe it should for the reasons identified, we have one opportunity to get this legislation right,” Sankey said. “If Congress passes a bill and it’s signed into law, we won’t be returning to D.C. in a year or two asking and receiving help to correct the gaps that exist. That’s why it’s important that these common-sense areas be addressed now before the bill becomes law.”

On Playoff expansion, Sankey’s stance has not changed much, if at all. He continued to stress the need for leaders to understand the interest fans and broadcasters have in a 24-team bracket along with the impact it would have on the regular season. He also raised questions about whether CFP games could or should overlap and the academic/physical aspects of another change to the calendar.

“We also need to know what is the actual interest from fans and from media entities in an expanded College Football Playoff,” Sankey said. “How do we respect the academic calendar and respect the well-being of our student athletes? When we went from four to 12, those questions were answered during the consideration process.”

The future of conference championship games is a related part of the conversation. Sankey said the league will hold its game this season and that the SEC has “contracts and plans in place well beyond that.” But the conference also has “time for consideration” if the CFP format changes again.
